title: Making the most of leftovers: Improved privacy amplification for quantum key distribution
authors: Matthew Simon Tan, Bartosz Regula, Marco Tomamichel
abstract: The amount of secret key that can be obtained from a quantum key distribution run depends on both the physically observed error rates and the mathematical bounds used to certify security. For finite datasets, conservative bounds force users to discard a substantial fraction of the potentially available key. Here we further refine and extend the privacy amplification bounds achievable through the recent leftover hash lemma of Regula and Tomamichel [arXiv:2603.04493] and incorporate them into the security analysis of quantum key distribution based on entropic uncertainty relations. This improves on state-of-the-art key rates in finite-block regimes, certifying more secret key from the same experimental data without changes to the protocol, and outperforming techniques based on entropy accumulation. The results illustrate how sharper mathematical estimates can directly increase the usable output of a quantum communication system.
summary: This paper significantly improves the theoretical limits on key extraction in Quantum Key Distribution by refining the privacy amplification bounds using the leftover hash lemma. The authors derive a sharper bound on the state deviation, which translates directly into a higher certified secret key rate from the same experimental data. This work highlights how precise mathematical analysis can boost the practical utility of quantum communication systems.
main_problem: The paper aims to increase the amount of secret key extractable from a Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) run, especially when dealing with finite amounts of experimental data.
main_result: By refining privacy amplification bounds using the leftover hash lemma, the authors demonstrate a provable increase in the certified key rate compared to state-of-the-art techniques.
method: The core method involves refining the privacy amplification bounds by improving the bound on the trace distance between the actual state and the hashed state, which is then incorporated into the overall security analysis.
model_or_system: The analysis is applied to Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols, using security proofs based on entropic uncertainty relations and finite-block analysis.
key_observables: Secret key length ($\ell$), conditional smooth min-entropy ($H_{\epsilon}^{\min}(X|E)_{ho}$), and the trace distance $\Delta(ho, H)$.
important_parameters: Smoothing error parameter ($\epsilon$), total security error ($\epsilon_{	ext{tot}}$), and the block size ($m$).
main_assumptions: The analysis builds upon existing frameworks using entropic uncertainty relations and assumes the applicability of the refined leftover hash lemma for 2*-universal hash families.
figures_summary: Figures compare finite-block key rates ($\ell/m$) versus block size ($m$) for various error rates, showing the advantage of the new LHL over older bounds.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by refining the bound on the trace distance $\Delta(ho, H)$ (using variational expressions and inequalities), establishing a sharper Leftover Hash Lemma (Theorem 1), and finally combining this into a comprehensive finite-key security proof (Theorem 2) to determine the maximum certified key length.
why_interesting: While focused on QKD, the rigorous mathematical techniques for bounding information leakage and extracting randomness from noisy quantum measurements are fundamental to understanding the limits of quantum communication protocols.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Finite-block key rates. Secret key bits per round, ℓ/𝑚, are plotted for quantum bit error rates 𝑄= 1% and 2.5%. The entropic uncertainty relation (EUR) curves compare the new and old leftover hash lemmas (LHL) with exact sampling. Their inputs are ideal BB84 overlap 𝑐= 1/2, 𝜀tot = 10−10 and 𝜀com = 0.01. Circles show the corresponding key rates from the refined analysis of the Rényi entropic accumulation theorem [AHT25] due to Goh and Tan [GT26]. For each EUR curve, the protocol parameters 𝑘, 𝑛, 𝑡, 𝑄tol are optimised to maximise ℓ. Table 2 gives example parameter values for the crossed point. See Section III and Appendix D for details on the numerical analysis.

Figure 2: Key extraction from short blocks. (a) Secret key length for 𝑚∈{1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000} at 𝜀tot = 10−10. Lines show EUR + new LHL with exact sampling; circles show the REAT results [GT26], with negative rates displayed at zero. (b) Minimum block size 𝑀0 yielding one secret bit, for 𝜀tot ∈ {10−10, 10−8, 10−6}. Both panels’ EUR calculations use ideal BB84 overlap 𝑐= 1/2, 𝜀com = 0.01 and assumed leakage coefficients (𝜉1, 𝜉2) = (1.13, 3.82) at every quantum bit error rate (QBER). Panel (a) uses 𝜅= 4/3; (b) retains the full bound of Theorem 1. We optimise 𝑘, 𝑛, 𝑡, 𝑄tol to maximise ℓat fixed 𝑚in (a), and minimise 𝑚 with ℓ≥1 in (b). The cross identifies the example in Table 2.
